9. Mr. Mandal, the learned Advocate for the appellants, however argued referring to the impugned judgment that, learned Special Tribunal has, in fact, convicted and sentenced the appellants on mere surmise and conjectures. He was not definite in his observation and finding as to whether the alleged arms were in fact recovered from the possession of the accused appellants and that is why he has used in judgment the words অনুমতি এ পরোক্ষভাবে "here and there". In this connection it is submitted by the learned Advocate for the appellants that the prosecution must prove its case by the reliable and sufficient evidence beyond all reasonable doubt. And the onus of proving of the case is always on prosecution which never shifts and that the finding of the court must be laid on legal evidence. In this connection he has argued that in a criminal case presumption of innocence should always be in favour of the accused until he is found guilty from evidence, and when a case after conviction of the accused comes before a court of appeal after admission of the said appeal for hearing that presumption of innocence continue still the appellate Court on scrutiny of the evidence on record upholds the conviction. In support of his contention he has relied on two decisions of Criminal Indian jurisdiction, one in the case of Emperor vs. Nur Ahmed reported in AIR 1934 Allahabad 842 wherein it has been observed as follows: 

 "The powers of the Appellate Court are exactly the same in the case of an order of acquittal as in the case of an order of conviction. The duty of the appellate Court is to review the entire evidence to make up its mind upon that evidence and to reverse the decision of the lower Court if it be satisfied upon a consideration of the evidence that the decision is unjustified. The presumption of innocence with which the accused starts continues right through until he is held to be guilty by the final Court of appeal. If he is acquitted by the Court of first instance the presumption of innocence of course remains. The presumption of innocence is absolute. It is not strengthened by an acquittal nor weakened by a conviction in the trial Court." 

 "In a criminal appeal it is for the Crown to establish that the judgment of the trial Court is right. The appellate Court must remember that the presumption of the innocence of the accused still persists and that the appellate Court has to satisfy itself that the judgment of the Magistrate was right. Where in the judgment of the appellate Court nether the points for determination, nor the reasons for the decision have been set out but it merely deals with the case for the defence only by seeming to answer, in a somewhat desultory and disjointed manner, the arguments of the defence, it is not a case of an error in a judgment, but that is a case of there being no application to a case of this description". 

 10. Mr. Mandal, the learned Advocate for the appellants, does not dispute the propriety of law and the spirit of section 134 of the Evidence Act but his contention is, that in case of conviction based on a single witness it must be that the single witness is wholly and fully reliable. In support of his contention he has referred to a decision of mine in the case of Ashok Kumar Saha vs. State, reported in 46 DLR 229 and then further contends that in the instant case PW 1 is not a witness of that quality. He stated something in his deposition regarding recovery of the alleged arms in presence of local witnesses, but who were at least 100 in number at the place of occurrence but of them only 2 or 3 witnesses were cited as witnesses and 2 of them were made seizure-list witnesses but they have come before the court and categorically stated that they did not see any recovery of the arms. These witnesses namely, PWs 2 and 3, belied the prosecution case and seriously negative the credibility of PW 1 and, according to his own version, he (PW 1) received a wireless message from the Thana about the possession of the arms of the accused appellants at the place of occurrence but nobody comes to the court and supports him in this matter. Most surprising aspect of this case is that, according to the version of the PW 1, he was on patrol duty along with his other constables, whom are specifically named in the FIR, but none of them were made witness in this case. This non-production of these witnesses and also another seizure list witness casts serious doubts about prosecution case. The facts and circumstances of the case have given rise to an adverse presumption against the prosecution case under section 114 of the Evidence Act. It may be remembered that PW 1 is the informant and a member of the Police force and he having lodged the FIR is undoubtedly interested so that accused are convicted and punished. So, his evidence cannot but he taken with a grain of salt in the facts and circumstances of the case. In this connection Mr. Mandal has relied on a decision in the case of Gaziur Rahman vs. State reported in 11 BLD 11 which again is a decision of mine and submitted that PW 1 being the informant he is naturally interested and his evidence in the facts and circumstances of the case should not be relied on and acted upon in convicting the appellants without corroboration by any other evidence. In support of his contention he has also relied on a decision in the case of Lasmon Das vs. State of Punjab reported in AIR 1970 (SC) 450. Thus having given our anxious consideration to all aspects of this case and to the evidence on record and the decisions cited above we are of the view that it is not safe to rely on the evidence of the sole witness PW 1 the informant in this case to base conviction of the accused appellant and in the facts and circumstances of the case the false implication of the appellants at the instance of their enemies cannot be ruled out and, in that view of the matter, that the appellants should be given benefit of doubt and their conviction and sentence cannot be found to be legal and proper which should be set aside.
